task.goal: Help a household share one bicycle without last-minute conflicts.
hard_constraints: Three adults use one bike and a paper calendar; no tracking app.
Keep personal trip destinations private and allow emergency use.
Compare missed trips, idle time and coordination effort for two weeks.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Reserve only the time you need
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use the paper calendar as the sole booking record. Each adult writes an initial and departure–return window as soon as a trip becomes likely; destinations and purposes stay private. The first entry holds the bike. Overlapping requests require an agreed swap before either person relies on the bike. Release cancelled bookings promptly, and keep the key in one agreed place whenever the bike is home. Allow a realistic return buffer.

This changes the outcome by exposing conflicts early while leaving unbooked hours available to everyone. It requires people to check the calendar and return on time; uncertain schedules and habitual early booking could undermine it. No materials beyond the calendar, a writing implement and existing key are needed.

An emergency overrides an ordinary booking when the bike is home: tell the affected adult if reachable, mark an estimated return, and disclose no destination. A bike already away cannot be recalled reliably with these resources.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare seven days of the current routine with seven days of reservations, matching weekdays. On the calendar, tally intended trips missed because the bike was unavailable, approximate daylight hours the bike sat unused, and minutes spent checking, discussing or recording arrangements. Include measurement effort consistently in both weeks. Also mark booked windows that went unused. The mechanism is doubtful if missed trips do not fall, or if unused reservations and coordination effort rise substantially. Two weeks provide a preliminary comparison; different trip demand or emergencies could explain differences.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Rotate predictable priority periods
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Divide each day into morning, afternoon and evening periods on the calendar. Assign priority to the three adults in a repeating rotation, shifting the starting adult each day. The priority adult marks whether they need their period by the preceding evening; otherwise it becomes open. Another adult may reserve a released period by initialling it. Trips must finish before the next claimed period, including a return buffer. Keep the key in a fixed place when the bike is home.

Predictable ownership reduces repeated negotiation and distributes desirable periods across people. Only initials and times appear, keeping destinations private. Implementation needs one initial calendar setup and brief daily checks. It assumes most trips fit the periods and that adults can sometimes shift departure times. Long or inflexible trips require an explicit swap, and unequal demand may make equal priority inefficient.

Emergency use takes precedence whenever the bike is present, with notice to the displaced adult where possible and an estimated return on the calendar. It cannot guarantee access while someone is riding.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use the current routine for week one and rotating priority for week two. Record daily missed intended trips caused by bike availability, approximate unused daylight hours, and coordination minutes. Mark whether each missed trip fell inside someone else's claimed but unused period. Before starting, agree what increase in effort or idle time would outweigh fewer missed trips. Reject or revise the routine if rigid periods themselves cause repeated misses or claimed periods sit empty. Compare matching weekdays, while noting that a single week per condition cannot establish a reliable causal effect.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Allocate conflicts by fewest recent rides
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Each evening, adults enter only their next day's desired departure–return windows and initials on the calendar. Nonoverlapping requests stand automatically. For an overlap, priority goes to whoever has completed the fewest bike trips during the preceding seven days, counted from small completion ticks on the calendar. Break ties using a rotating initial order written at the top. Resolve conflicts that evening; later requests fit around confirmed windows unless everyone affected agrees to change them. Cancel unused requests promptly and return the key to its agreed place.

The mechanism gives a clear, inspectable answer to competing requests while compensating people who have used the shared bike less. It needs a short evening check and one tick per completed outing, without recording destinations. It assumes ride counts are an acceptable fairness measure: a short outing and a long outing count equally, so this may fit poorly where needs differ sharply. It also exposes usage frequency, although personal destinations remain private.

An emergency overrides the allocation when the bike is home, without requiring disclosure of its purpose. Notify displaced users if possible and mark the expected return. Emergency rides also receive completion ticks.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare one week of the current routine with one week using the rule. Tally bike-related missed intended trips, approximate unused daylight hours and coordination minutes on the calendar. Inspect each contested window: was the decision settled the evening before, and did the winner actually use it? The rule fails its basic purpose if conflicts still require last-minute bargaining, or if fewer rides merely redistribute missed trips without an acceptable fairness benefit. Ask each adult privately whether the allocation felt workable; two weeks cannot establish longer-term fairness.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Fit flexible trips around fixed ones
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a brief evening scheduling check to fit the next day's trips together. Each adult writes only initials, expected bike-use duration including a return buffer, and earliest departure/latest return. Someone with a fixed appointment can give a narrow window without explaining why. No destinations or purposes are recorded.

Together, place the least flexible trips first, then fit flexible trips into the remaining gaps. Confirm actual departure–return times on the calendar before ending the check. Entry order gives no priority. If two trips cannot both fit, ask whether either person can shift; if neither can, use a rotating tie-break initial and acknowledge the unresolved missed trip in advance. Late requests use remaining gaps or require agreement from affected adults.

The working principle is to use scheduling flexibility to preserve trips that would otherwise collide. This differs from awarding an overlap to the first claimant: a flexible request can move so both people ride. It assumes adults know roughly how long they need and that some trips can shift. If everyone's timing is fixed, this routine offers little benefit and may add discussion.

Implementation needs the existing calendar, key, an available pen, and a short shared check. Keep the key in one agreed place when home and cross out cancelled allocations. An emergency may override the schedule whenever the bike is present, without disclosing its destination or purpose; mark an expected return and notify displaced users if reachable. Access cannot be guaranteed while someone is riding.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
For seven days, retain the current routine; for the next seven, use flexible-window scheduling. In both weeks, tally daily intended trips missed because the bike was unavailable, approximate hours the bike was home and unused within the same agreed daily observation period, and total person-minutes spent coordinating and recording measurements. Compare matching weekdays and note total requested trips.

During the trial week, mark each occasion when shifting a flexible trip allowed both requests to happen. Inspect after three days: if no requests can shift and discussion takes longer, the proposed mechanism has little support. After two weeks, judge whether fewer misses justify any added effort or idle time. This is a preliminary comparison; changing demand and emergencies can explain differences.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Use a waiting queue with bounded loans
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use the calendar as a same-day waiting queue rather than allocating future time slots. An adult who wants the bike writes their initial and latest useful departure time, without a destination or purpose. Cross out requests that expire or are withdrawn. When the bike returns, the earliest still-active entry gets the next turn; skip anyone who is not ready to leave. With no waiting entries, anyone may take it.

Agree on a normal maximum loan length that accommodates common local trips. Before leaving, the borrower checks the queue and writes an expected return. If someone is waiting, the borrower must return within that limit. A longer outing requires agreement from those already waiting. Return the key to one agreed place and tell the next waiting adult that the bike is back when practical.

The mechanism is a work-conserving queue: the bike keeps moving between ready users, while bounded loans stop one discretionary outing from blocking several others. It could suit a household whose trips are mostly short and whose departure times tolerate some waiting. It assumes adults can check the calendar, communicate at home, and honor return estimates. Fixed appointments, long essential trips, and requests entered while the bike is already away remain weaknesses. Implementation needs only calendar space, an existing writing implement, the key, and a brief agreement on the loan limit.

An emergency goes ahead of the queue whenever the bike is home. Mark an expected return and notify displaced adults if reachable; no explanation or destination is required. Emergency access cannot be guaranteed while the bike is away.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Keep the current routine for seven days, then try the queue for seven. In both weeks, tally bike-related missed intended trips, approximate home-and-unused hours during the same daily observation period, and total person-minutes spent coordinating and recording. Count trips abandoned because the loan limit was too short as missed trips. Compare matching weekdays and note demand and emergencies. Inspect the first three contested returns: did the next ready adult actually get the bike promptly? Repeated empty handoffs, excessive checking, or more missed trips would undermine the mechanism. The two-week comparison is preliminary because demand may differ.

EXPAND.title: Give turns to people ready to leave
EXPAND.proposal:
Use a ready-now queue instead of advance reservations. Agree a maximum ordinary outing length that covers common local trips. An adult joins by writing their initial on today's calendar only when ready to depart; nobody holds a place for a later departure. When the bike is home, the first waiting adult takes the key, crosses out their queue entry and writes an expected return time. Someone who is no longer ready loses their place. After returning the bike and key to the agreed location, a rider may rejoin behind anyone waiting.

This removes a step that sharing does not always require: predicting trips and negotiating future windows. It prevents speculative reservations from blocking an available bike and gives waiting users a clear order. It assumes adults are often near home and ordinary trips fit a mutually acceptable duration. Someone with a fixed appointment cannot rely on future availability; if such trips are common, this approach is unsuitable. Trips exceeding the agreed limit require agreement from the other adults before departure.

Only initials, queue order and return times appear; destinations remain private. An adult may declare an emergency without explaining its purpose and take the next available bike ahead of the queue. Mark an estimated return and notify waiting adults in person where possible. A bike already away remains unavailable. If a return is late, the queue stays in order, but nobody should treat the estimate as a guarantee. Implementation uses the existing calendar, its writing implement and lock key.
EXPAND.experiment: One adult maintains the trial totals. Compare seven days of first-entry time reservations with seven days of the ready-now queue, matching weekdays. Each adult records daily bike-related missed trips, approximate bike-idle hours within the same agreed observation period, and coordination minutes, including recording and waiting to settle access. Separately tally outings prevented by the duration limit. Stop the queue trial early if an essential fixed-time trip is missed because future access could not be secured, and retain the partial results. Reject it if missed trips increase or reduced administration merely shifts effort into waiting. Demand differences make this a preliminary comparison.

EXPAND.title: Fit flexible trips around immovable departure times
EXPAND.proposal:
Each evening, adults put tomorrow's requests on the calendar using only an initial, earliest possible departure, latest acceptable departure and maximum bike-use duration. A single departure time means that request cannot move. Nobody records a destination or explains why a time is fixed. One adult, rotating daily, spends at most five minutes arranging nonoverlapping outings within those limits, including agreed return buffers.

First try to fit every request by moving flexible outings around fixed ones. When all requests cannot fit, choose the arrangement serving the most outings; if equally good arrangements exclude different people, rotate whose request is left out. Each adult confirms their assigned time before relying on it. If agreement is not reached within five minutes, use a rotating priority order for that day's unresolved requests. Later requests fit into remaining gaps unless affected adults agree to a change.

The working principle is to change departure times within boundaries people have already accepted, rather than decide which overlapping reservation wins. Unlike first-entry booking, an early flexible request need not exclude a later immovable one. This requires some genuine flexibility and an acceptable estimate of outing duration. It can disadvantage long outings, so the trial must inspect who loses access as well as total misses.

Cross out cancelled outings promptly. Return the bike and key to their agreed location after each outing. An emergency overrides the plan whenever the bike is home; mark an estimated return and notify displaced adults in person where possible, without requiring a destination or justification. If the bike returns late, affected adults explicitly revise the remaining times before relying on them. No app or additional equipment is needed.
EXPAND.experiment: A named adult totals seven days of first-entry reservations and seven days of flexible-window scheduling, matching weekdays. Record daily bike-related missed trips, approximate idle hours over the same observation period, and all coordination minutes. Count misses separately for each adult and for longer outings. Inspect whether rearranging flexible requests actually enabled trips that first-entry booking would have excluded. Stop and revert if anyone's confirmed trip is repeatedly displaced or the five-minute planning limit is exceeded on three evenings. Prefer the simpler comparator if total misses do not fall, or if gains depend on unacceptable extra planning or concentrating misses on one adult. Two weeks cannot establish performance under every demand pattern.

EXPAND.title: Reservations with a clear release and late-return rule
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: “Reserve only the time you need.” Keep initialled departure–return reservations, first-entry priority, agreed swaps, return buffers, prompt cancellations and a fixed home for the key. Record no destinations.

Change the procedure when a booking does not start or finish as expected. Agree a short departure grace period. The reservation holder must mark a delayed departure before that grace expires; otherwise the booking lapses. Another adult may then borrow only if they can return before the next reservation, including its buffer. This releases abandoned bookings without requiring someone to locate the holder.

If the bike is missing at a reserved departure, the waiting adult marks the trip as at risk and decides whether to wait or abandon it; the calendar does not imply availability. The returning rider owns recovery: on arrival, check the calendar, give the next affected adult first access, and revise any remaining overlap with them before departing again. Until they accept a change, their existing reservation remains in force. If repeated lateness makes return estimates unreliable, suspend advance borrowing across another person's booking and revert to explicit agreement for those transitions.

An emergency takes precedence when the bike is home. The emergency rider writes an estimated return and informs displaced adults if reachable, without disclosing a destination or justification. An absent bike cannot be guaranteed. This needs only the existing calendar, its writing implement and key. Compared with ordinary reservations, it may recover unused time but introduces a grace-period check and can disadvantage someone delayed unexpectedly.
EXPAND.experiment: One adult totals seven days of ordinary reservations followed by seven days with the release and recovery rules. Each adult records bike-related missed intended trips, estimated idle hours during the same daily observation period, and coordination minutes, including measurement effort. Also mark bookings released after the grace period and any resulting dispute or missed trip. Compare matching weekdays and misses per adult. Stop automatic release after the first disputed release that causes a missed trip; require explicit cancellation for the remaining trial while retaining the late-return rule. Keep the upgrade only if recovered access or fewer misses justify the extra checks. Different demand across weeks limits the conclusion.

EXPAND.title: Flexible scheduling with a five-minute confirmation fallback
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: “Fit flexible trips around immovable departure times.” Retain next-day requests containing initials, earliest and latest departures, maximum duration and return buffers. A rotating daily planner has five minutes to fit requests, first seeking an arrangement that serves everyone, then the most outings; rotate exclusions between equally good arrangements. No destination or explanation of a fixed time is required.

Change the confirmation handoff. Before rearranging, treat already confirmed times as binding. The planner may propose changes, but each affected adult must initial acceptance within the same five-minute session. The planner owns the proposal until every affected adult accepts; silence is not acceptance. If the session is interrupted or time expires, discard unaccepted changes and preserve confirmed times. Resolve only new, unresolved overlaps by the written rotating priority order, leaving any request that cannot fit explicitly unconfirmed. An adult who misses the session can later claim a free gap or negotiate a swap, but cannot rely on an unconfirmed request.

This prevents a partly communicated rearrangement from becoming two incompatible plans. It preserves the mechanism of fitting flexible trips around fixed ones, but may lose some efficient arrangements when adults cannot meet. If joint confirmation regularly fails, fall back to first-entry reservations rather than extending the planning session. Cancel promptly, keep the key in its agreed place, and explicitly revise affected times after a late return. Emergency use overrides bookings when the bike is home, with an estimated return and notice where possible; destinations stay private. Only the existing calendar, writing implement and key are needed.
EXPAND.experiment: A named adult totals seven days of first-entry reservations and seven days of this scheduling routine. Record daily missed intended trips due to bike availability, estimated idle hours over a fixed observation period, and all coordination minutes. Separate misses by adult and longer outings. Mark proposed rearrangements that were accepted, discarded or interrupted, and inspect whether accepted changes enabled additional trips. Revert to first-entry reservations if confirmation fails on three evenings, the five-minute limit is exceeded on three evenings, or anyone is repeatedly displaced from confirmed times. Compare fewer misses against planning effort and concentrated exclusions. Two weeks offer only preliminary evidence.

EXPAND.title: Lend against the next return deadline
EXPAND.proposal:
Use return deadlines rather than exclusive booking windows. Each adult writes an initial and the next time they need the bike physically home, without a destination or purpose. A deadline does not reserve the preceding hours. Whenever someone takes the key, they must be able to complete their outing and an agreed buffer before the earliest outstanding deadline; they write their expected return. Thus short outings can use the bike while another adult's later need remains protected.

At their deadline, the requesting adult either takes the bike and crosses out the claim or releases it. They must check that their own outing will finish before the next person's deadline. If successive needs cannot both fit, the affected adults must agree a change before either relies on access; use a rotating initial order for an unresolved clash, and mark the other trip unconfirmed. Do not claim deadlines merely to hold the bike idle. If a deadline arrives and its owner is absent, allow a short agreed grace period, then release it.

The rider owns returning the bike and key on time. If it is late, preserve the next adult's claim when it arrives and settle remaining clashes before another departure. If duration cannot be estimated confidently, borrow only after agreement from the next deadline holder; without agreement, leave the bike home. An emergency may take the available bike immediately, recording an estimated return and notifying affected adults where possible. No destination disclosure is needed, and emergency access cannot be guaranteed while the bike is away.

This removes the need to reserve an entire future interval merely to secure a departure. It could reduce idle gaps compared with reservations, but requires reliable duration estimates and may produce more negotiation when needs are tightly spaced. It uses only the existing calendar, writing implement and key.
EXPAND.experiment: One adult totals seven days of ordinary reservations and seven days of deadline lending. Record bike-related missed intended trips, estimated idle hours over identical daily observation periods, and coordination minutes, including recording effort. Mark outings fitted before a deadline, late returns that displaced someone, and clashes left unconfirmed. Inspect an ordinary short outing with ample slack and one with insufficient buffer before trying the routine. Stop deadline lending after two deadline misses caused by overlong borrowing, or immediately if an adult finds the uncertainty unacceptable; revert to reservations. Prefer it only if access improves enough to justify estimation and negotiation effort. Demand differences and the short trial leave its benefit uncertain.
